lines.text: of her tumultuous life? Does she not also disclose decay and
death? We may certainly affirm that all decay and death
are swallowed up in the great, heedless circling of her life,
that every death in her midst only marks the transition to
new life, and that in the total sphere of nature there prevails
order, peace and intelligibility of pattern. But do we see
deep enough into her to know whether this circling of her
life, in which each individual specimen constantly falls as a
sacrifice to the whole, has ultimate meaning and purpose?
Again, the worship of the powers of nature constantly runs
the risk of being transformed into its opposite: into awe and
terror of her unfathomable and sinister secrets. To many a
questing mind it has seemed that the gay colours in which her
laws bedeck themselves grew pale, and that these laws took
on the appearance of an impassive, compulsive force: to them
the order of the cosmos was imprisoning. No doubt Jesus can
speak of the heavenly Father who causes His sun to shine on
the evil and the good, and His rain to fall on the just and the
unjust, but the poet who does not know this heavenly Father
enthroned above nature sees the matter otherwise and says:
"For unfeeling is nature: the sun shines on the evil and the
good, and the moon and the stars illuminate the path of the
evil-doer as of the upright."
At best there is operative in nature an uncanny, un-
fathomable power which can kindle no response in our heart.
And Klopstock, who was not only a great German poet, but
also a great Christian poet, addresses God present in nature
thus: "Without Him who has loved me and sacrificed Himself
for me, I could not be Thine! Without Him the thought of
Thine all-pervading preserice were terrible, an anguished
fear of the all-powerful Unknown."
Further, this simple faith in nature fails to recognize not only
the sinister mystery of nature herself, but also the character-
istic essence of man. For man too, of course, is a part of
nature; yet not merely a part of nature. As the Scripture
expresses it, he was created in the image of God, i.e. in his
inmost self he is not nature but spirit. Unlike the plants and
